newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-AUSTRALIAN BATSMEN TIGHTEN GRIP ON ASHES.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-AUSTRALIAN BATSMEN TIGHTEN GRIP ON ASHES.

text.p: Australia took command of the fifth test at Trent Bridge on Thursday, cruising to 302 for three on the opening day to virtually end England's hopes of reclaiming the Ashes.
Trailing 2-1 in the six-match series and needing victory, England were in trouble from the moment they lost the toss for the fifth successive time in ideal batting conditions.
Australian captain Mark Taylor admitted he had thoughts of 1989, when he and the current coach Geoff Marsh batted throughout the first day at the same venue to put on 301.
This time Taylor (76) and Matthew Elliott (69) stayed until 40 minutes after lunch, putting on 117, before falling to Andy Caddick and Dean Headley respectively.

"It was an important toss, more so than the other four, and I'm delighted that we've made good use of it," said Taylor. "I'd like to make as many as we can. Another day like today would be fantastic."
The Australian captain's innings must have come as a relief to him after scores of one, two, one and nought since his century in the first test.
He also became only the sixth Australian to pass 6,000 runs in test cricket, while Elliott reached 500 for the series and 1,000 on the tour.
"I remember playing against West Indies at the start of my career and thinking I might not make 60," said Taylor. "So it's a great honour."
Greg Blewett weighed in with 50 before becoming the first test victim of 19 year-old debutant Ben Hollioake, caught one-handed by wicketkeeper Alec Stewart.
With fellow debutant Adam Hollioake in action at the other end and Steve Waugh coming in to join his twin Mark, a capacity crowd was treated to the unusual spectacle of brothers bowling to brothers.
Not surprisingly, the experienced Australians emerged from the fraternal feud on top, sharing an unbroken partnership of 77. Mark Waugh ended the day on 60.

On a good batting strip, England skipper Mike Atherton threw both Hollioakes into the action early despite their modest record with the ball in county cricket -- only 20 wickets between them all season.
But neither man could contain the free-scoring Australians after strike bowler Devon Malcolm, recalled for the injured Darren Gough, failed to make any impact.
"I couldn't fault the commitment or effort," said England coach David Lloyd. "We didn't get the ball in the right area often enough.
"I wouldn't say we're out of it but it's a lot of hard work from now on."
